DART-ITS: Detailed Mathematical Theory, Novel Algorithm Design, and System Architecture

Doctoral research development — Stage 2

Your research direction is now defined:

  • Research domain: Multiple university subjects.

  • Target population: All university students, including undergraduate, master's, and doctoral students.

  • AI technologies: Deep Learning + Reinforcement Learning.

  • Primary research focus: Deep Knowledge Tracing + Adaptive Teaching.

  • Development priority: Mathematical theory and system architecture before software implementation.

This choice leads to a more ambitious research problem than building a tutor for a single course.

I recommend developing DART-ITS as a subject-independent, hierarchical, multi-domain intelligent tutoring framework.

The key scientific challenge is that students studying mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, and other subjects do not share the same knowledge structures. However, they share certain learning characteristics:

  • Knowledge acquisition.

  • Knowledge retention.

  • Forgetting.

  • Learning difficulties.

  • Conceptual dependencies.

  • Responses to instructional interventions.

  • Learning progression.

Your architecture should separate these common learning characteristics from subject-specific knowledge.

This separation will be one of the most important design principles in your doctoral research.

PART I — MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION

1. Define the research problem

Traditional intelligent tutoring systems often model students through individual knowledge components and their interaction histories.

However, a university-wide intelligent tutoring system must address four interconnected problems:

  1. How to represent knowledge across different academic subjects.

  2. How to estimate the evolving knowledge state of each student.

  3. How to predict the impact of different teaching actions.

  4. How to select instructional actions that maximize long-term learning outcomes.

I propose formulating DART-ITS as a hierarchical partially observable reinforcement learning problem.

The system will contain three interacting models:

Three mathematical models of DART-ITS

Model 1 — Knowledge Representation Model

Represents concepts, prerequisites, academic subjects, and their relationships.

Gs=(Vs,Es,Ws)G_s=(V_s,E_s,W_s)Gs​=(Vs​,Es​,Ws​)

Model 2 — Deep Student State Model

Estimates the student's knowledge, retention, learning ability, and uncertainty.

z^t=fθ(x1:t,Gs)\hat{z}_t=f_\theta(x_{1:t},G_s)z^t​=fθ​(x1:t​,Gs​)

Model 3 — Adaptive Instructional Policy

Selects the next teaching action using reinforcement learning.

at∼πϕ(a∣bt)a_t\sim\pi_\phi(a\mid b_t)at​∼πϕ​(a∣bt​)

The student interacts with the selected instruction, producing new observations and updating all three models.

The three models should be designed together, rather than as independent software modules.

3.4 Knowledge evolution model

Knowledge does not change randomly. It evolves through learning activities, practice, feedback, and forgetting.

A candidate model is:

Ki,t+1(c)=Ki,t(c)+ΔKi,t(c)−Fi,t(c)K_{i,t+1}^{(c)} = K_{i,t}^{(c)} + \Delta K_{i,t}^{(c)} - F_{i,t}^{(c)}Ki,t+1(c)​=Ki,t(c)​+ΔKi,t(c)​−Fi,t(c)​

Where:

  • ΔK\Delta KΔK: Knowledge acquisition.

  • FFF: Knowledge forgetting.

A possible learning acquisition function is:

ΔKi,t(c)=σ(W1at+W2dt+W3pt+W4zi,t)\Delta K_{i,t}^{(c)} = \sigma( W_1 a_t+ W_2 d_t+ W_3 p_t+ W_4 z_{i,t} )ΔKi,t(c)​=σ(W1​at​+W2​dt​+W3​pt​+W4​zi,t​)

Here:

  • ata_tat​: Teaching action.

  • dtd_tdt​: Instructional difficulty.

  • ptp_tpt​: Practice characteristics.

  • σ\sigmaσ: Sigmoid activation.

A candidate forgetting function is:

Fi,t(c)=Ki,t(c)(1−e−λcΔT)F_{i,t}^{(c)} = K_{i,t}^{(c)} \left(1-e^{-\lambda_c\Delta T}\right)Fi,t(c)​=Ki,t(c)​(1−e−λc​ΔT)

Where λc\lambda_cλc​ is a concept-specific forgetting parameter and ΔT\Delta TΔT is elapsed time.

This is an initial modeling hypothesis. Actual learning and forgetting dynamics should be estimated from longitudinal student data rather than assumed to follow this exact equation.

PART II — NOVEL REINFORCEMENT LEARNING ALGORITHM

4. Formulate adaptive teaching as a POMDP

The second major scientific contribution is the intelligent instructional decision engine.

The system should not simply recommend the next question based on a student's current score.

It should select the instructional action that is expected to produce the greatest long-term learning improvement.

This is naturally modeled using a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP).

4.1 POMDP definition

Define the tutoring environment as:

P=(S,A,O,T,Z,R,γ)\mathcal{P}= (\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O}, T,Z,R,\gamma)P=(S,A,O,T,Z,R,γ)

Where:

Symbol

Meaning

S\mathcal{S}S

Hidden student learning states

A\mathcal{A}A

Instructional actions

O\mathcal{O}O

Observable student interactions

TTT

State transition model

ZZZ

Observation probability model

RRR

Reward function

γ\gammaγ

Discount factor

The true knowledge state is not directly observable.

For example, a student might answer a question correctly by guessing rather than understanding the concept.

Therefore, the tutoring system should maintain a belief distribution:

bt(s)=P(St=s∣o1:t,a1:t−1)b_t(s)=P(S_t=s\mid o_{1:t},a_{1:t-1})bt​(s)=P(St​=s∣o1:t​,a1:t−1​)

The belief state is updated after each new student interaction.

In practical implementation, the deep student model will provide a compact representation of this belief state.

4.2 Define the instructional action space

I recommend creating an instructional action hierarchy.

Hierarchical instructional action space

Level 1 — Instructional strategy

  • Teaching

  • Practice

  • Assessment

  • Remediation

  • Review

Level 2 — Teaching method

  • Concept explanation

  • Worked example

  • Guided example

  • Hint

  • Interactive problem

  • Knowledge test

Level 3 — Instructional parameters

  • Difficulty

  • Explanation depth

  • Number of exercises

  • Hint intensity

  • Time allocation

This hierarchy is important because a multi-subject system will have a very large action space.

For example, the action "provide an example" means something different in mathematics, physics, and computer programming.

The system should select a teaching strategy first and then select a subject-specific instructional implementation.

4.4 Proposed reinforcement learning algorithm

I recommend developing an algorithm provisionally named:

HA-DARP: Hierarchical Adaptive Deep Reinforcement Policy

The proposed algorithm will combine:

  1. Deep student-state estimation.

  2. Hierarchical action selection.

  3. Long-term reward optimization.

  4. Educational constraints.

  5. Uncertainty-aware instructional decisions.

I suggest using PPO as the initial policy optimization foundation, rather than developing an entirely new RL optimizer from scratch.

The doctoral novelty can be concentrated in the hierarchical state-action design and learning-oriented policy mechanism.

The policy is:

πϕ(at∣bt,et)\pi_\phi(a_t\mid b_t,e_t)πϕ​(at​∣bt​,et​)

For hierarchical actions:

πϕ(at∣bt)=πϕ1(gt∣bt)πϕ2(mt∣gt,bt)πϕ3(pt∣mt,gt,bt)\pi_\phi(a_t\mid b_t) = \pi_{\phi_1}(g_t\mid b_t) \pi_{\phi_2}(m_t\mid g_t,b_t) \pi_{\phi_3}(p_t\mid m_t,g_t,b_t)πϕ​(at​∣bt​)=πϕ1​​(gt​∣bt​)πϕ2​​(mt​∣gt​,bt​)πϕ3​​(pt​∣mt​,gt​,bt​)

Where:

  • gtg_tgt​: Instructional strategy.

  • mtm_tmt​: Teaching method.

  • ptp_tpt​: Instructional parameters.

This structure makes the action space easier to manage across different subjects.

5. Design the learning-oriented reward function

The reward function is potentially one of the most important original components of your research.

A poorly designed reward function can produce a tutoring system that appears intelligent but does not actually improve education.

For example, an agent that receives a reward whenever the student answers correctly may repeatedly choose easy exercises.

We need a reward that reflects meaningful learning.

5.1 Proposed multi-objective reward

I propose:

rt=w1ΔKt+w2ΔRt+w3Gt−w4Dtex−w5Ct−w6Vt\begin{aligned} r_t={}& w_1\Delta K_t+ w_2\Delta R_t+ w_3G_t\\ &-w_4D_t^{ex} -w_5C_t -w_6V_t \end{aligned}rt​=​w1​ΔKt​+w2​ΔRt​+w3​Gt​−w4​Dtex​−w5​Ct​−w6​Vt​​

Where:

ΔRt\Delta R_tΔRt​

GtG_tGt​

DtexD_t^{ex}Dtex​

CtC_tCt​

VtV_tVt​

w1,…,w6w_1,\ldots,w_6w1​,…,w6​

The reward should be evaluated over meaningful learning periods, not merely after every individual question.

For instance, a review exercise might not immediately improve the test score but could significantly improve retention over several weeks.

5.2 Knowledge gain calculation

One possible mastery improvement measure is:

ΔKt=Kt+1−Kt\Delta K_t= K_{t+1}-K_tΔKt​=Kt+1​−Kt​

However, directly rewarding changes in the neural model's estimated mastery can create a serious problem: the agent might learn to exploit errors or inconsistencies in its own student model.

Therefore, I recommend using two complementary measurements:

  • Model-estimated mastery improvement for frequent policy feedback.

  • Independently assessed mastery improvement for periodic reward validation.

The second should be measured using carefully designed assessment questions, not just the questions selected by the agent.

5.3 Retention reward

Knowledge retention should be measured after a time delay.

Let:

Rt(c)=P(correct response to concept c after delay ΔT)R_t^{(c)}= P(\text{correct response to concept }c \text{ after delay }\Delta T)Rt(c)​=P(correct response to concept c after delay ΔT)

The retention reward can then be based on the change in this probability.

This gives the system an incentive to review material at appropriate intervals.

5.4 Educational safety constraints

I recommend adding constraints to the RL problem.

For example:

max⁡πEπ[∑tγtrt]subject toP(dt>dmax⁡)≤ϵP(prerequisite violation)≤δAssessment quality≥qmin⁡\begin{aligned} \max_{\pi}\quad& \mathbb{E}_{\pi} \left[\sum_t\gamma^t r_t\right]\\ \text{subject to}\quad& P(d_t>d_{\max})\leq\epsilon\\ & P(\text{prerequisite violation})\leq\delta\\ & \text{Assessment quality}\geq q_{\min} \end{aligned}πmax​subject to​Eπ​[t∑​γtrt​]P(dt​>dmax​)≤ϵP(prerequisite violation)≤δAssessment quality≥qmin​​

The system should avoid:

  • Assigning advanced topics without prerequisite knowledge.

  • Repeating the same ineffective teaching action indefinitely.

  • Excessively increasing question difficulty.

  • Selecting materials that are not appropriate for the student's academic level.

  • Treating uncertain knowledge estimates as confirmed mastery.

These constraints can be implemented through action masks, constrained policy optimization, or a safety layer between the RL agent and the teaching engine.

Proposed research contribution 3: A hierarchical, uncertainty-aware and education-constrained reinforcement learning policy for adaptive instructional decision-making.

6. Knowledge transfer between academic subjects

This is an especially important research challenge because you selected multiple university subjects.

Consider a student studying:

  • Mathematics.

  • Physics.

  • Electrical engineering.

  • Computer science.

These disciplines share some mathematical foundations, but they do not share all concepts.

For example, differentiation is important in calculus, control systems, and optimization.

Your system should be able to recognize these relationships.

6.1 Cross-domain knowledge representation

Let the global knowledge graph be:

G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E)

Instead of keeping completely independent subject graphs, the system can connect related concepts across disciplines.

For example:

linear-tec.jp

We can define a cross-domain relationship:

wij=sim⁡(ei,ej)⋅ρijw_{ij}= \operatorname{sim}(e_i,e_j) \cdot \rho_{ij}wij​=sim(ei​,ej​)⋅ρij​

Where:

  • ei,eje_i,e_jei​,ej​: Concept embeddings.

  • sim⁡\operatorname{sim}sim: Semantic or structural similarity.

  • ρij\rho_{ij}ρij​: Strength of the educational relationship.

Importantly, similarity alone does not establish prerequisite equivalence. Cross-domain links should be validated by curriculum experts.

6.2 Shared and domain-specific student representations

I recommend separating student learning into two representations:

zi,t=zi,tglobal⊕zi,tdomainz_{i,t}= z_{i,t}^{global} \oplus z_{i,t}^{domain}zi,t​=zi,tglobal​⊕zi,tdomain​

Where:

  • zglobalz^{global}zglobal: General learning characteristics.

  • zdomainz^{domain}zdomain: Subject-specific knowledge.

The global representation might capture learning history and general learning efficiency.

The domain-specific representation captures knowledge of individual subjects.

This allows the system to reuse relevant information without transferring mastery incorrectly.

For example, being good at calculus should not automatically imply that a student understands electrical circuit theory.

6.3 Domain adaptation

For a new subject with limited training data, use transfer learning:

θj=θshared+Δθj\theta_j= \theta_{shared}+\Delta\theta_jθj​=θshared​+Δθj​

Where:

  • θshared\theta_{shared}θshared​: Shared parameters.

  • Δθj\Delta\theta_jΔθj​: Subject-specific adaptation.

This is a form of parameter-efficient domain specialization.

You can investigate whether shared learning representations improve performance when moving from well-supported subjects to subjects with limited interaction data.

Proposed research contribution 4: A shared-subject and domain-adaptive student modeling architecture that supports multiple university disciplines while preserving subject-specific knowledge.

I recommend using a modular, layered architecture with seven primary services.

7.2 Detailed service design

Service 1 — User and Course Management

Responsibilities:

  • Student registration.

  • Academic-level management.

  • Course enrollment.

  • Subject selection.

  • Learning history.

  • Instructor permissions.

Suggested database entities:

Plain text
Student Instructor University Department Course Subject Enrollment AcademicLevel

Service 2 — Learning Interaction Service

This service manages the student's interaction with the system.

It records:

Plain text
Interaction_ID Student_ID Course_ID Subject_ID Concept_ID Question_ID Response Correctness Response_Time Hint_Usage Timestamp

It should also support learning events such as video completion, reading activities, and practical exercises.

Service 3 — Knowledge Representation Service

This service maintains the educational knowledge graphs.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Concept definitions.

  • Prerequisite relationships.

  • Subject relationships.

  • Difficulty levels.

  • Learning objectives.

  • Assessment mappings.

I recommend a graph database such as Neo4j for the initial prototype, although PostgreSQL can also store graph-like structures for a smaller implementation.

Service 4 — Deep Student Modeling Service

This is the first AI engine.

It receives student interactions and returns:

Plain text
Student_ID Concept_ID Mastery_Estimate Retention_Estimate Learning_Efficiency Uncertainty Model_Version

It should also support historical state reconstruction for research experiments.

Service 5 — Reinforcement Learning Service

This is the second AI engine.

It receives the estimated student state and instructional context.

It returns:

Plain text
Student_ID Selected_Strategy Selected_Teaching_Method Difficulty_Level Content_ID Policy_Confidence Decision_Reason

The decision reason should be generated from auditable policy inputs and rules, rather than relying on an unverified explanation of the neural network's internal reasoning.

Service 6 — Adaptive Teaching Service

This service delivers the selected learning activity.

For example:

  • Concept explanation.

  • Worked example.

  • Practice exercise.

  • Hint.

  • Remedial lesson.

  • Assessment.

It should maintain a separation between the decision policy and the actual educational content.

Service 7 — Analytics and Evaluation Service

This service provides:

  • Student progress dashboards.

  • Course-level analytics.

  • Learning improvement measurements.

  • Model performance reports.

  • RL policy evaluation.

  • Research experiment tracking.

Four computational stages

  1. Hierarchical concept representation.

  2. Deep temporal student-state estimation.

  3. Uncertainty-aware hierarchical policy selection.

  4. Constrained instructional optimization and state updating.

9.1 Algorithm execution

Plain text
Algorithm: DART-ALGO INPUT: Student profile U Academic subject D Knowledge graph G Learning objectives O Educational resources E INITIALIZATION: Load shared neural model Load subject-specific model Initialize student knowledge state Initialize RL policy FOR each learning interaction t: 1. COLLECT STUDENT DATA Observe question, response, time and hint usage 2. UPDATE KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION Encode the current concept Identify prerequisite relationships 3. ESTIMATE STUDENT STATE Apply graph encoder Apply temporal Transformer Estimate mastery and retention Estimate predictive uncertainty 4. CONSTRUCT RL STATE Combine student state Add course context Add academic level Add available resources 5. SELECT INSTRUCTIONAL STRATEGY Select teaching strategy Select teaching method Select instructional parameters 6. APPLY EDUCATIONAL SAFETY CHECK Verify prerequisites Verify difficulty constraints Verify curriculum requirements 7. DELIVER INSTRUCTION Provide learning material or assessment 8. OBSERVE STUDENT RESPONSE Record new interaction 9. UPDATE LEARNING MODEL Update knowledge state Evaluate learning improvement Update retention estimates 10. UPDATE RL POLICY Record transition Calculate reward Update policy during approved training END FOR OUTPUT: Student learning profile Adaptive learning path Knowledge mastery report Learning outcome evaluation

An important distinction: the RL policy should generally be trained offline or in controlled training environments. It should not automatically modify its parameters after every live student response. This separation improves reproducibility and prevents uncontrolled experimentation on students.

9.2 Training procedure

I suggest a three-stage training process.

Three-stage model training

  1. Stage 1 — Supervised deep learning

    Train the knowledge-tracing model on historical educational interaction datasets.

    Objective: Predict student performance and estimate knowledge states.

  2. Stage 2 — Offline reinforcement learning

    Train instructional policies using historical interaction trajectories, a validated simulator, and off-policy evaluation.

    Objective: Learn educationally appropriate instructional strategies.

  3. Stage 3 — Controlled policy refinement

    Test the policy in a controlled environment, followed by approved university experiments.

    Objective: Validate whether the learned policy improves real student learning.

9.3 Deep learning loss function

I recommend using a multi-task objective:

LDL=αLKT+βLRET+ηLUNC+μLREGL_{DL}= \alpha L_{KT} +\beta L_{RET} +\eta L_{UNC} +\mu L_{REG}LDL​=αLKT​+βLRET​+ηLUNC​+μLREG​

Where:

  • LKTL_{KT}LKT​: Knowledge-tracing prediction loss.

  • LRETL_{RET}LRET​: Retention prediction loss.

  • LUNCL_{UNC}LUNC​: Uncertainty calibration loss.

  • LREGL_{REG}LREG​: Regularization loss.

For knowledge tracing, binary cross-entropy is a reasonable starting point:

LKT=−∑t[ytlog⁡(p^t)+(1−yt)log⁡(1−p^t)]L_{KT}= -\sum_t [y_t\log(\hat p_t) +(1-y_t)\log(1-\hat p_t)]LKT​=−t∑​[yt​log(p^​t​)+(1−yt​)log(1−p^​t​)]

For retention, use a separate prediction target measured through delayed assessments.

For uncertainty calibration, compare predicted confidence against actual prediction errors using appropriate probabilistic metrics.

9.4 Reinforcement learning loss function

Using PPO as the baseline optimizer:

LPPO=Lpolicy−cvLvalue+ceLentropyL_{PPO}= L_{\text{policy}} -c_vL_{\text{value}} +c_eL_{\text{entropy}}LPPO​=Lpolicy​−cv​Lvalue​+ce​Lentropy​

Where:

  • LpolicyL_{\text{policy}}Lpolicy​: Clipped policy objective.

  • LvalueL_{\text{value}}Lvalue​: Value function loss.

  • LentropyL_{\text{entropy}}Lentropy​: Exploration regularization.

  • cv,cec_v,c_ecv​,ce​: Hyperparameters.

The constrained version should additionally account for educational safety costs, for example through a Lagrangian formulation:

max⁡ϕ[JR(ϕ)−λJC(ϕ)]\max_\phi \left[ J_R(\phi)-\lambda J_C(\phi) \right]ϕmax​[JR​(ϕ)−λJC​(ϕ)]

Here, JRJ_RJR​ is expected learning reward, JCJ_CJC​ is expected constraint cost, and λ\lambdaλ is a nonnegative multiplier.

This is a proposed optimization framework; its stability and effectiveness need experimental validation.

PART IV — RESEARCH EXPERIMENTS AND VALIDATION

10. Experimental research design

I recommend designing the experiments around the four central scientific claims.

Experiment

Research question

Comparison

E1

Does hierarchical deep modeling improve knowledge estimation?

BKT, DKT, Transformer KT

E2

Does uncertainty improve instructional decisions?

Standard vs uncertainty-aware policy

Rule-based, DQN, PPO, HA-DARP

Does multi-domain adaptation improve generalization?

Independent subject models vs shared model

10.1 Experiment E1 — Knowledge tracing

Test the proposed student model using different academic subjects.

Measure:

  • AUC.

  • Accuracy.

  • Log loss.

  • Brier score.

  • Calibration.

  • Performance on students with limited historical interactions.

The most important result should be whether the proposed model generalizes to students and courses that were excluded from training.

10.2 Experiment E2 — Uncertainty-aware decision-making

Compare two versions:

  • Model A: Estimates mastery without explicit uncertainty.

  • Model B: Estimates mastery and uncertainty.

Measure whether the uncertainty-aware model selects better diagnostic questions and avoids inappropriate instructional decisions.

10.3 Experiment E3 — Adaptive teaching

Compare:

  • Fixed instructional sequence.

  • Rule-based teaching.

  • DQN.

  • PPO.

  • Proposed hierarchical policy.

Measure long-term learning reward, knowledge retention, prerequisite violations, and instructional efficiency.

10.4 Experiment E4 — Multi-subject generalization

This is essential for your chosen research scope.

Train on several subjects and test on a held-out subject.

For example:

Training subjects

Computer Science

Mathematics, Computer Science, Physics

Engineering

This tests whether the model learns transferable learning representations rather than simply memorizing subject-specific interaction patterns.

However, cross-subject knowledge transfer and generalization of learning behavior must be evaluated separately.

PART VII — CRITICAL RESEARCH DECISIONS

14. What should actually be novel in your PhD?

I want to emphasize an important distinction.

Your dissertation should not claim that Transformer + GNN + PPO is automatically a novel algorithm. These technologies already have extensive research histories.

The novelty should come from a rigorously defined and validated combination of research mechanisms.

I would prioritize the following four contributions:

Four proposed doctoral contributions

Contribution 1

Hierarchical Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing

A shared and subject-specific neural representation for student knowledge across multiple university disciplines.

Contribution 2

Uncertainty-Aware Student State Estimation

A model that jointly estimates mastery, retention, and uncertainty, including under sparse student interaction data.

Contribution 3

Hierarchical Constrained Reinforcement Learning

An instructional policy that selects teaching strategies and teaching methods while satisfying educational constraints.

Contribution 4

Long-Term Learning Optimization

A multi-objective decision framework that considers knowledge acquisition, retention, transfer, and instructional efficiency.

Develop the complete mathematical specification of DART-HKT and HA-DARP.
